ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Arts, University of Nottingham.
Upon following the link, potential participants were first presented with an introduction and ethics details.
In order to take part, participants were required to have English as either their first or second language; this was also confirmed in a demographic questionnaire as part of the study.
Two hundred and seventy two participants took part in the study.
Participants were aged between 16 and 61 (mean age: 24.9; SD: 8.3).
Participation was voluntary, and participants were entered into a prize draw for online shopping vouchers.
Participants gave informed consent at the start of the study, and were free to withdraw at any time without penalty.
Participants were presented with the corresponding set of seven emoticons and asked to select any that they would personally use in the given type of context.
The sets of emoticons presented to participants were taken from a study by Thompson and Filik (2016).

Participants were presented with an array of emoticons along with a reference emoticon.
Random intercepts for participants were included in all models.
For each of the following contexts, the intentionally unsuitable emoticon was consistently rated as highly unsuitable, confirming that participants were using the scale appropriately.
For the :p emoticon, L1 participants were significantly less likely to rate the ;p emoticon as equivalent (0.23) than L2 participants were (0.39) (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.25;0.79], p = .023).

Across all context types, L2 participants were consistently more likely to use kaomoji than L1s, and also gave them consistently higher suitability ratings, though these patterns were not always statistically significant.

Although participants were asked to judge broad context types rather than individual messages, the illustrative example that was provided for each context type may have influenced how that context was interpreted.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .1", "ps > .5", "ps > .1", 
"ps > .8", "ps > .1", "ps < .05"), Text = c("For all other emoticons, there were no significant differences between L1 and L2 (all ps > .1).", 
"All other ps > .5.", "All ps > .1.", "In both general positive and very positive contexts, L1s and L2s do not differ in their ratings to this emoticon (ps > .8), with both groups rating its suitability for any type of positive context as neutral.", 
"Across all four reference emoticons, there were no other individual emoticons for which L1 and L2 users of English significantly differed in their equivalence ratings (all ps > .1).", 
"Each difference category significantly differed from all other difference categories (all Holmadjusted ps < .05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .787", "ps > .1", "ps > .5", "ps > .1", "ps > .8", "ps > .1"), Sentence = c("The overall likelihood of emoticon use across the various contexts was the same for L1 (mean: 0.19) and L2 (0.19) users of English (OR = 1.03, 95% CI [0.85;1.24], p = .787).", "For all other emoticons, there were no significant differences between L1 and L2 (all ps > .1).", "All other ps > .5.", "All ps > .1.", "In both general positive and very positive contexts, L1s and L2s do not differ in their ratings to this emoticon (ps > .8), with both groups rating its suitability for any type of positive context as neutral.", "Across all four reference emoticons, there were no other individual emoticons for which L1 and L2 users of English significantly differed in their equivalence ratings (all ps > .1)." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Emoticons can visually differ in various minor ways.

This includes presence or absence of an element, like the 'nose' or 'tear' in the :-) and :'( emoticons, differences in orientation, as in the :) versus (: emoticons, or a change to an element, such as the 'eyes' in the :) versus ;) emoticons.
It is unclear which types of variation impact meaning, or whether the visual scale of variation predicts the degree of impact on meaning.
We investigated emoticon use, contextual suitability, and perceived meaning equivalence across positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts.
Given that emoticons can clarify message intent and may be used as a compensatory tool in a second-language, we also compared L1 (n = 151) and L2 (n = 119) users of English.
Utilising emoticons that were produced by participants in earlier research, a series of ratings and selections revealed systematic differences in the effects of visual variations.

Changes to the nose element and rotation had relatively little impact on perceived meaning, whereas mirroring and changes to the eyes or mouth had progressively greater effects, with mouth variation producing the greatest impact.
L1 and L2 users patterned closely in overall usage, contextual suitability judgements, and interpretations of meaning equivalence.
However, differences emerged for particular variants, especially interpretations of winking and tongue-out emoticons, as well as greater L2 use and acceptance of uprightoriented kaomoji.

These findings suggest that aspects of emoticon meaning are systematically influenced by constituent elements, but are partly conventionalised within language communities, with implications for cross-linguistic digital communication and digital literacy.
Emoticons are a common, and now widely-researched, feature of computer-mediated communication.
They incorporate expressive faces, such as the sideways-oriented smiling :) or upright-oriented crying T.T emoticons, as well as some objects and animals, such as the heart <3 or fish ><> emoticons.
text.formatted: They incorporate expressive faces, such as the sideways-oriented smiling :) or upright-oriented crying T.T emoticons, as well as some objects and animals, such as the heart <3 or fish ><> emoticons.

text.text: Broadly speaking, sideways-oriented emoticons originated in English-speaking Western culture, while upright emoticons, such as the Japanese kaomoji, originated in Eastern cultures or languages (Dresner & Herring, 2010).
text.formatted: Broadly speaking, sideways-oriented emoticons originated in English-speaking Western culture, while upright emoticons, such as the Japanese kaomoji, originated in Eastern cultures or languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dresner & Herring, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Emoticons have a wide range of functions that go well beyond the original conceptualisation as "emotion icons".

In some cases, emoticons may be used to express particular emotions, but more commonly they are used as pragmatic markers (Dresner & Herring, 2010; Skovholt et al., 2014), to clarify message intent (Thompson & Filik, 2016), or to reduce potential ambiguity (Filik et al., 2016).

text.text: A pair of studies by Thompson and Filik (2016) revealed a high degree of consistency in emoticon choices for various context types, including several forms of sarcasm.
text.formatted: A pair of studies by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Thompson and Filik (2016)</ref> revealed a high degree of consistency in emoticon choices for various context types, including several forms of sarcasm.

text.text: Emoticons continue to persist alongside the more pictorial emoji, despite the high popularity of the latter.

Since emoticons are constructed from ASCII characters, they have a high degree of visual consistency across platforms, devices, and software, while emoji can vary significantly across each of these contexts (Miller et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Since emoticons are constructed from ASCII characters, they have a high degree of visual consistency across platforms, devices, and software, while emoji can vary significantly across each of these contexts <ref type="bibr">(Miller et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This stability may be an important factor when aiming to clearly signal message intent.
At the same time, emoticons can be easily modified by users.

Although emojis can exhibit small variations between each other, users still select them from a limited set of prerendered pictorial designs that the user cannot edit. Fricke et al. (2024) demonstrated that minor visual variations between emoji can impact perceived meaning, though the user-driven variations in emoticons have not been investigated.

(2024)</ref> demonstrated that minor visual variations between emoji can impact perceived meaning, though the user-driven variations in emoticons have not been investigated.

text.text: Unlike the typically fixed emoji, users can add, remove, or alter individual elements of an emoticon, such as adding a 'nose' or changing the shape of the 'mouth' element.
Some of these changes may have a purely decorative effect, while others may impact an emoticon's perceived meaning or contextual suitability.

Previous findings suggest that, while certain emoticons frequently appear in the same contexts, such as both ;) and :p being common in sarcastic messages, others that are superficially very similar appearance tend towards different contexts, such as :) for general positive contexts and ;) for sarcastic or flirty contexts (Thompson & Filik, 2016).
text.formatted: Previous findings suggest that, while certain emoticons frequently appear in the same contexts, such as both ;) and :p being common in sarcastic messages, others that are superficially very similar appearance tend towards different contexts, such as :) for general positive contexts and ;) for sarcastic or flirty contexts <ref type="bibr">(Thompson & Filik, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that certain variations and alterations to emoticons influence perceived meaning or purpose, while others do not.

Given that prior research has identified emoticons as helpful for clarifying communicative intent and has also reported more frequent use in L2 contexts, it is important to understand whether these variations and alterations are used and interpreted consistently, and whether L1 and L2 language users share the same interpretations.
The function of emoticons as indicators of message intent means they have greater communicative relevance in contexts where there is a higher chance for misunderstanding.
Both irony and sarcasm are highly ambiguous (Filik & Moxey, 2010), making them particularly prone to misunderstanding and hence are often investigated within studies of emoticon function.
text.formatted: Both irony and sarcasm are highly ambiguous <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Filik & Moxey, 2010)</ref>, making them particularly prone to misunderstanding and hence are often investigated within studies of emoticon function.

text.text: This ambiguity arises as both irony and sarcasm involve saying one thing while communicating the opposite of the surface form.
For example, a person may say "That's an amazing idea!"
with the intention of communicating "That idea is terrible".
Sarcasm is a form of irony with many functions, but it is typically critical in tone, and often used when targeting a person (Kreuz & Glucksberg, 1989).
text.formatted: Sarcasm is a form of irony with many functions, but it is typically critical in tone, and often used when targeting a person <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kreuz & Glucksberg, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: If the sarcastic or ironic intent is not detected by the person receiving the message, they will drastically misinterpret it.

The added complexity in decoding the intent of a sarcastic message can increase the processing difficulty (Filik et al., 2014; Kaakinen et al, 2014; urcan & Filik, 2016), so supportive cues Ț to intent are valuable.
text.formatted: The added complexity in decoding the intent of a sarcastic message can increase the processing difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Filik et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kaakinen et al, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">urcan & Filik, 2016)</ref>, so supportive cues Ț to intent are valuable.

text.text: Sarcasm is highly frequent in communication despite these added difficulties (Gibbs, 2000; Whalen et al., 2012) and has been shown to have diverse functions (Colston, 2007; Dews et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Sarcasm is highly frequent in communication despite these added difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gibbs, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Whalen et al., 2012)</ref> and has been shown to have diverse functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Colston, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dews et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: In spoken language, intonation can be a cue to the presence of sarcasm (Thompson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In spoken language, intonation can be a cue to the presence of sarcasm <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Thompson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For written forms of language, emoticons can ease the processing difficulty by highlighting the presence of non-literal or implied meaning (Derks et al., 2008), or by specifically marking sarcastic intent (Thompson & Filik, 2016).
text.formatted: For written forms of language, emoticons can ease the processing difficulty by highlighting the presence of non-literal or implied meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Derks et al., 2008)</ref>, or by specifically marking sarcastic intent <ref type="bibr">(Thompson & Filik, 2016</ref>).

text.text: Yet, as noted above, emoticons are still open to a degree of interpretation.
Emoticons have also been shown to be a useful tool in second language contexts.
In group text chats between native and non-native speakers, Vandergriff (2014) found that nonnative speakers made more frequent use of emoticons than native participants.
They suggest that this higher usage may help to compensate for lower proficiency, even if that difference in proficiency is minor.
Emoticons can in a sense be used as a backup strategy when a user is uncertain of the exact connotations of a word.
Similar conclusions were reached by Aragon et al. (2014), with the increased use of emoticons by non-native users corresponding to a relatively lower amount of text production in the same chats.
text.formatted: Similar conclusions were reached by <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Aragon et al. (2014)</ref>, with the increased use of emoticons by non-native users corresponding to a relatively lower amount of text production in the same chats.

text.text: However, others have found that both first language (L1) and second language (L2) users tend to show an increased use of emoticons when there is a lower degree of lexical variation (Shaikh et al., 2017). Togans et al. (2021) also found that English proficiency did not impact the use of emoticons.
text.formatted: However, others have found that both first language (L1) and second language (L2) users tend to show an increased use of emoticons when there is a lower degree of lexical variation <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Shaikh et al., 2017)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Togans et al. (2021)</ref> also found that English proficiency did not impact the use of emoticons.

text.text: Some research has suggested that there may be cultural or linguistic difference in emoticon preferences. Park et al. (2014) note that within 'individualistic' cultures, there is a preference for sideways-oriented emoticons, while in 'collectivist' cultures, there is a preference for upright-oriented emoticons.
text.formatted: Some research has suggested that there may be cultural or linguistic difference in emoticon preferences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Park et al. (2014)</ref> note that within 'individualistic' cultures, there is a preference for sideways-oriented emoticons, while in 'collectivist' cultures, there is a preference for upright-oriented emoticons.

text.text: Of course, the individualistic-collectivist distinction overlaps strongly with the languages in which sideways and upright emoticons first emerged; hence it is uncertain whether this is truly a matter of culture, rather than frequency of exposure within a given language.
Others have reported that the connotations given to an emoji can vary depending on the language in which it is used (Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Others have reported that the connotations given to an emoji can vary depending on the language in which it is used <ref type="bibr">(Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: What is not known, is whether users from different language backgrounds vary in their interpretation of emoticons when they are using the same language.

Given that second language users often struggle with subtle differences in meaning and with messages that depend heavily on context, the inherently ambiguous nature of sarcasm again makes it a noteworthy area for investigation.
As previously detailed, one function of emoticons is to clarify message intent.

For contexts that are highly ambiguous or easily misunderstood, such as the aforementioned sarcastic or ironic contexts, the usefulness of emoticons for clarification is particularly evident (Thompson & Filik, 2016).
text.formatted: For contexts that are highly ambiguous or easily misunderstood, such as the aforementioned sarcastic or ironic contexts, the usefulness of emoticons for clarification is particularly evident <ref type="bibr">(Thompson & Filik, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Although research shows an increase in emoticon usage in L2 contexts, it is important to understand whether second language users are able to make effective use of emoticons to clarify message intent, especially in contexts that are more likely to benefit from the added clarity an emoticon can provide.

It is clear that emoticons can provide a useful and effective strategy for ensuring clarity of message intent, particularly in ambiguous or sarcastic contexts, and are useful as a compensatory or supplementary tool when communicating in a non-native language.
They also can be readily modified by users, resulting in many subtle variations, with only some of these being semantically meaningful.
Here, we present a study to examine how a range of visual variations to emoticons may impact their use, contextual suitability, and perceived equivalence of meaning.
We also consider how these might differ between native and nonnative speakers of English.
Our aim is to explore how visual variations in emoticons might impact their use and interpretation.
We will present participants with emoticons that have been shown to appear frequently in positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts (Thompson & Filik, 2016).
text.formatted: We will present participants with emoticons that have been shown to appear frequently in positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts <ref type="bibr">(Thompson & Filik, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Our assumption is that if a pair of emoticons can be routinely used in the same context, their meaning must overlap to some degree; we will explore to what degree their meanings overlap by examining patterns of usage, perceptions of contextual suitability, and judgements of equivalence.

This will involve an exploratory analysis, but broadly, in terms of individual emoticon elements, we expect the mouth and eyes to be more significant for meaning than noses, as the former are the more expressive parts of a face, and the latter have been shown to be frequently omitted by emoticon users (Thompson & Filik, 2016).
text.formatted: This will involve an exploratory analysis, but broadly, in terms of individual emoticon elements, we expect the mouth and eyes to be more significant for meaning than noses, as the former are the more expressive parts of a face, and the latter have been shown to be frequently omitted by emoticon users <ref type="bibr">(Thompson & Filik, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Other types of differences, such as rotating or inverting an emoticon, may not have a great impact on meaning, since they do not change, add, or remove any of the individual elements that are likely to contribute to an emoticon's overall meaning.

By understanding which elements contribute to emoticon meaning, and their relative importance in comparison to each other, these findings have the potential to improve translation software, sentiment analysis, natural language processing, and language teaching.
We will also explore how native and non-native speakers of English use and interpret emoticons across positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts.

Given that emoticons are established as a useful tool for clarification (Dresner & Herring, 2010; Skovholt et al., 2014; Thompson & Filik, 2016), and are frequently used by non-native speakers communicating with native speakers (Aragon et al., 2014; Vandergriff, 2014), it is important to know whether these two groups actually intend the same thing when using particular emoticons.
text.formatted: Given that emoticons are established as a useful tool for clarification <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dresner & Herring, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Skovholt et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Thompson & Filik, 2016)</ref>, and are frequently used by non-native speakers communicating with native speakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aragon et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vandergriff, 2014)</ref>, it is important to know whether these two groups actually intend the same thing when using particular emoticons.

text.text: Awareness of any differences can be used to support cross-cultural or cross-linguistic communication, and to inform language learning and digital literacy.

In general, we expect that L1 and L2 users of English will share similar interpretations of many emoticons, though agreement may decrease for less frequent emoticons, since less exposure would lead to less fixed definitions.

Given that sarcastic contexts are the most complex and potentially ambiguous of those in this study, and emoticons are often used for clarification, we would expect a higher frequency of emoticon use in sarcastic contexts.
This effect may be even more pronounced for L2 participants, who have been shown to increase emoticon use in non-native contexts.
In this study we utilised ratings and multiple choice selections to investigate how visual variation in emoticons impacts their meaning.
We examined five broad context types and within each we explored patterns of usage, perceptions of contextual suitability, and judgements of meaning equivalence.

Recruitment was carried out via participation mailing lists maintained by departments at the University of Glasgow and University of Nottingham, which encompass a highly diverse population of both students and the general public.
Anyone interested in taking part could follow a link to the study, hence this constituted a self-selecting opportunity sample.
Upon following the link, potential participants were first presented with an introduction and ethics details.
In order to take part, participants were required to have English as either their first or second language; this was also confirmed in a demographic questionnaire as part of the study.
Two hundred and seventy two participants took part in the study.
Two were excluded and their data erased due to declining the ethics statement, leaving two hundred and seventy participants in the following analyses.
Participants were aged between 16 and 61 (mean age: 24.9; SD: 8.3).
Sixty nine percent identified as female, and 30% as male; 1 participant identified as non-binary, and 1 as agender.
Our aim was to explore the use and interpretation of emoticons in English, as well as to compare use and interpretation between native speakers (L1) and non-native speakers (L2) of the language.

Our aim was not to examine interactions between English and any other specific language -simply to compare how L1 and L2 users of a given language may align or differ in their conceptions of emoticon variations.
The large samples allow us to explore broad patterns across L1 and L2 English populations.

However, the L2 group was not designed to explore how specific language background variables may contribute to observed patterns, Investigation of variables such as knowledge of other languages in the L1 group, and language family or proficiency of the L2 group, could be examined in future studies, after the broader effects of L1 versus L2 use and interpretation are established.
In total, there were 151 participants in the L1 English group and 119 in the L2 English group.
Participation was voluntary, and participants were entered into a prize draw for online shopping vouchers.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Arts, University of Nottingham.
Participants gave informed consent at the start of the study, and were free to withdraw at any time without penalty.
The study consisted of multiple choice and ratings questions, divided into three main sections, detailed below.
All parts of the study were presented in individual sections within a single Typeform survey.
The first section examined emoticon usage in five specific context types: general positive, very positive, general negative, very negative, and sarcastic.

The second section prompted ratings of suitability for emoticons in the same five types of context used in the first section.

Here, instead of a grid of all options, participants were presented with one emoticon at a time and asked to rate its suitability for the given context type.

text.text: The third section examined meaning equivalence between emoticons.
Participants were presented with an array of emoticons along with a reference emoticon.
Their task was to select any emoticons they judged as having the same meaning as the given reference emoticon.
Participants could alternatively select 'none'.

As before, we chose emoticons that were used with high frequency in positive, negative, and sarcastic messages in Thompson and Filik's (2016) production study, with the most frequently used emoticons serving as our reference emoticons.

text.text: A final section asked demographic information, such as age, gender identity, and native language, as well as which messaging apps participants frequently used, and how often they used emoticons in their messages.
The study was run online using the Typeform survey platform and could be completed on any computer, phone, or tablet with internet access.
Following the ethics statement, participants moved through the sections outlined above.
Selections and ratings were given by either clicking or tapping the appropriate response.
Trials were presented in a set order, though the array of options provided within each trial were displayed in a random order.
An example of a 'selection' type trial is given in Figure 1.

text.text: At the end of the study there was an option to leave an email address for entry into the prize draw.
The study typically took around 10 minutes to complete.
All data were analysed in R (version 4.3.3; R Core Team, 2024).

Binary data (usage and meaning equivalence) were analysed using generalised linear mixed-effects models with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) and ordinal data (suitability) were analysed using cumulative link mixed models with the ordinal package (Christensen, 2023).

text.text: In each analysis, participant response was modelled as a function of the fixed effects of native language and emoticon.
Native language had two levels (L1 vs L2); emoticon had seven levels, with the set of seven emoticons being specific to each context type.
Holm-adjustment was used to correct for multiple comparisons within each model.
Random intercepts for participants were included in all models.
Model outcomes and pairwise comparisons were calculated using the emmeans package (Lenth, 2018).

text.text: Across these meaning equivalence responses, we observed a general tendency for emoticons that differ only by the addition of a nose element to receive high equivalence ratings, while alterations to the mouth element resulted in noticeably lower equivalence ratings.

text.text: To explore this observed pattern further, we modelled how various elements and differences impact equivalence ratings.
First, we coded each emoticon for the types of differences they featured relative to their reference emoticon.
The categories were: differences in the nose element; differences in the mouth element; differences in the eyes element; mirroring of the emoticon; and, rotation of the emoticon.
A few emoticons fell into multiple categories, such as a difference in both nose and mouth elements relative to the reference.
Meanwhile, kaomoji are constructed so differently that individual differences cannot be separately identified.
Emoticons variants that fell into multiple categories (n = 2) and kaomoji (n = 7) were excluded because any potential effects could not be attributed to any one feature.

Only two variants involved more than one coded feature, and the possible feature combinations were not systematically represented, therefore interactions between variation types could not be reliably estimated.
As such, the analysis considers the degree to which each type of difference individually effects emoticon meaning.

text.text: In this study, we examined how visual variation in emoticons impacts their use, contextual suitability, and perceived meaning equivalence across positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts, as well as the extent to which these patterns are shared by L1 and L2 users of English.
Overall, results show the semantic impact of a variant depends not on the scale of the visual difference, but on the particular component or orientation that is altered.
Differences in the nose element and rotation had relatively little impact on perceived meaning, whereas mirroring and differences in the eyes and mouth had progressively greater effects.
L1 and L2 participants showed a high degree of alignment across all three measures, with differences concentrated in particular emoticons, especially winking, tongue-out, and upright-oriented forms.
However, contrary to our predictions, neither group had increased emoticon usage in sarcastic contexts relative to most other contexts.
Together, these findings suggest emoticon meaning variation has a systematic connection to constituent components and visual features.
L1 and L2 users of English largely share these connections, though some remain specific to particular language communities.
For the :) :( and :/ reference emoticons, each had three emoticon variants that were highly likely to be perceived as equivalent in meaning, with likelihoods over 0.74.
The :p emoticon, however, had only one highly equivalent emoticon variant, with all others having meaning equivalence likelihoods below 0.51.
As noted above, we had broad predictions as to which elements might contribute to meaning, though the study was largely exploratory.
In examining the perceived equivalence data, we observed general patterns whereby addition of a nose element had minimal impact on meaning, but altering mouth shape had far greater impact.
Meanwhile, some orientational differences appeared to have a notable impact on meaning, while others did not.
Through subsequent analysis, we explored the degree to which meaning was altered by differences in the nose, mouth, and eyes elements, and differences in rotation and mirroring orientations.
Overall, analysis revealed that minor visual variation can indeed impact perceived meaning, extending the findings of Fricke et al. (2024) from pictorial emoji to ASCII emoticons.
text.formatted: Overall, analysis revealed that minor visual variation can indeed impact perceived meaning, extending the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Fricke et al. (2024)</ref> from pictorial emoji to ASCII emoticons.

text.text: Analysis also showed that the types of difference significantly differed from each other in the degree of they had impact on perceived meaning.
Our expectation that eyes and mouth elements would impact meaning more than nose elements was borne out and aligns with frequency data in prior literature (Thompson & Filik, 2016).
text.formatted: Our expectation that eyes and mouth elements would impact meaning more than nose elements was borne out and aligns with frequency data in prior literature <ref type="bibr">(Thompson & Filik, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is notable that differences in the nose element do still impact perceived meaning, albeit to a vastly lower degree than both other elements.
Also of note, differences in the mouth element resulted in by far the greatest deviation in perceived meaning relative to the corresponding reference emoticons.

This may in part be influenced by the greater availability of options for the mouth element, which include curved parentheses, straight lines of varied angle, and several individual alpha-numeric characters, such as p or D or 0 (zero); whereas the eyes element is largely limited to colon or semicolon.
So, while the eyes still provide significant information, the mouth is the most productive element in generating distinct meanings.
Despite its impact, keeping mouth shape the same does not force an emoticon to retain the same meaning, since other additions or changes to other elements (such as the eyes) can impact the meaning.
However, making mouth shape different does have a very high likelihood of forcing a change in meaning.
Overall, this indicates that the shape of the mouth element is of particular importance in the correct interpretation of an emoticon's meaning.

In terms of the eyes element, while comparison of individual forms is too fine-grained for the present study, we can nonetheless descriptively see that a change from : to = had rather less impact than a superficially smaller change from : to ; did.
As such, it is not simply a change in shape that matters.
Whether this is due to salience, frequency of exposure, or aptness in representing a target facial expression, is a factor that should be investigated further.
As expected the nose element had by far the lowest likelihood of altering perceived meaning, at just 0.16.
However, in all observed cases, a change to the nose was via the addition of a nose relative to the reference emoticon.
It could be argued that simply adding to an emoticon has less impact on meaning than altering an element.
However, the only other instances of a purely additive change, which were the frowning brow in >:( and the tear in the :'( emoticon, greatly reduced perceived meaning similarity.
text.formatted: However, the only other instances of a purely additive change, which were the frowning brow in >:( and the tear in the :'( emoticon, greatly reduced perceived meaning similarity.

text.text: This supports the idea that the nose is the least expressive or meaningful element within an emoticon, hence its overwhelming likelihood of being omitted in emoticon production (Thompson & Filik, 2016).

text.text: Inverted versions of each reference emoticon typically had high meaning equivalence with their reference emoticon.

That is, emoticons that are visually identical other than their orientation are interpreted as closely equivalent in meaning, including the :) and (: emoticons, the :( versus ): emoticons, and the :/ versus /: emoticons.
However, the :p emoticon was far less likely to be seen as equivalent in meaning to the q: emoticon.

For both the :) and :( emoticons, the relationship to their inverted forms could be interpreted as either mirrored or rotated (i.e., mirroring or rotating 180 degrees would have the exact same visual result).
For the :/ emoticon, which displays the same pattern of meaning equivalence, its inverted form of /: is clearly rotated relative to the reference, with the mouth always lowered under the right eye.
Conversely, for the :p emoticon, which has notably less meaning equivalence with its q: inverted form, the nature of the inversion is clearly a mirroring.

Modelling emoticon variants where the type of inversion is unambiguous (either clearly rotated or clearly mirrored) revealed that the probability of impacting meaning is only 0.24 for rotations, but 0.49 for mirrorings.
These various inversions result in emoticons with the top of the face to the right, rather than the default leftward orientation.
Without a reference emoticon to compare them to, there would be no distinction between 'rotated' and 'mirrored'.
Since we observe a difference in the effect on perceived meaning between rotated and mirrored, it is likely they are being processed as derivations of the reference emoticon.
That being so, it would be interesting to explore why rotation has so much less impact than mirroring.

Taken together, the above suggests that when emoticons are encountered in a nondefault orientation, interpreting it as a mental rotation of the default is preferred over interpreting it as a mirroring.

Prior research has shown a difference in both the legibility (Erlikhman et al., 2017) and the processing (Martinaud et al., 2016) of rotated versus mirrored text, typically showing that rotated text is considered easier than mirrored, with the present findings suggesting this extends beyond text to emoticons.

text.text: At the same time, in neuroscientific literature, several studies have suggested emoticons are processed in similar ways to real human faces, such as in the identification of emotion (Yuasa et al., 2011), while others have shown either partial overlap or differences between emoticons and faces (see Aldunate & González-Ibáñez, 2017 for a review).
text.formatted: At the same time, in neuroscientific literature, several studies have suggested emoticons are processed in similar ways to real human faces, such as in the identification of emotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Yuasa et al., 2011)</ref>, while others have shown either partial overlap or differences between emoticons and faces (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Aldunate & González-Ibáñez, 2017</ref> for a review).

text.text: The broader picture seems to be that emoticons are treated as somewhat like both faces and text, while not entirely being either.

Given the visually subtle yet meaningful distinctions in elements and orientation, in order to correctly process and interpret emoticons, we need to acquire a sensitivity to which visual variations are meaningful and which visual variations are not meaningful.
This is comparable to other processes across cognitive and language development.

In English, for example, we need to learn that the written difference between 'e' and 'o' results in the representation of different sounds, but variations to the letter 'e' in terms of different fonts, handwriting, cases, colours, and so on, do not impact the sound being represented.
While individual emoticons are not restricted to any one language, their exact use and interpretation may vary across languages or cultures (Togans et al., 2021).
text.formatted: While individual emoticons are not restricted to any one language, their exact use and interpretation may vary across languages or cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Togans et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This has likewise been observed for emoji (Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This has likewise been observed for emoji <ref type="bibr">(Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, emoticon use has been shown to increase in L2 contexts, potentially as a compensatory or supportive tool (Aragon et al., 2014; Vandergriff, 2014).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, emoticon use has been shown to increase in L2 contexts, potentially as a compensatory or supportive tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aragon et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vandergriff, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For emoticons to be genuinely useful in these contexts, L1 and L2 users would need to be aligned in their usage and interpretations.
Our prediction was that L1 and L2 participants would pattern similarly, though the agreement might fall for frequent emoticons, and increased use might be exaggerated in sarcastic contexts.
We did observe a very high degree of alignment between the two groups, but the level of agreement did not change with emoticon frequency.
More surprisingly, reported likelihood of emoticon use actually fell for both groups in sarcastic contexts relative to most other contexts.
Broadly speaking, participants with L1 English or L2 English were highly consistent with each other.

The patterns of emoticon usage, judgements of contextual suitability, and interpretations of meaning equivalence all follow very similar overall distributions, with few individual emoticons revealing a significant difference between groups.
In each of the five context types, the emotions with the highest likelihood of use were the same for the two groups.
This was clearest in the positive conditions, where the top two emoticons were noticeably more likely to be used than the remaining options.
As well as usage, the emoticons most suited to each context were typically the same for the two groups, the pattern again being clearest in positive contexts.
The least suitable emoticons for each context were more variable, though in most cases this did not constitute a significant group difference.
Interpretations of meaning similarity between pairs of emoticons were also highly consistent between the language groups.
Overall, this indicates that in the majority of cases, L1 and L2 users of English use emoticons with the same frequency and interpret them in the same ways.

As such, the usefulness of emoticons as markers of intent or clarification (Dresner & Herring, 2010; Filik et al., 2016; Skovholt et al., 2014) and as a compensatory or supportive tool in L2 contexts (Aragon et al., 2014; Vandergriff, 2014) is supported by the current findings.
text.formatted: As such, the usefulness of emoticons as markers of intent or clarification <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dresner & Herring, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Filik et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Skovholt et al., 2014)</ref> and as a compensatory or supportive tool in L2 contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aragon et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vandergriff, 2014)</ref> is supported by the current findings.

text.text: While there are clear, high level similarities between participants with L1 and L2 English, there are some notable points of divergence.
The ;) emoticon was rated by L2s as quite suitable for both general positive and very positive contexts, whereas L1s rated it as unsuited to the former and neutral in latter.
While the smiling 'mouth' element appears positive, the winking eyes element appears to negate this interpretation for L1 English participants.
In a complementary pattern, L1s rate this same emoticon as one of the most suited to a sarcastic context, while L2s rate it as one of the least suitable.

Comparable differences have recently been reported for emoji, with winking emoji facilitating irony comprehension for US and UK participants, and smiling emoji being more effective for Chinese participants (Du, 2025; Du et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Comparable differences have recently been reported for emoji, with winking emoji facilitating irony comprehension for US and UK participants, and smiling emoji being more effective for Chinese participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Du, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Du et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests associations between winking forms and ironic or sarcastic intent may be stronger in some languages or cultures than others.
The current findings may reflect a related difference, although we did not distinguish between language and cultural background.
While the L1 and L2 groups rated the :p emoticon as having relatively neutral suitability for positive contexts, L1s were significantly more likely to use it themselves in a positive context.
This suggests that native speakers of English see this emoticon as rather more positive than non-native speakers do.
L1s also rated the same :p emoticon as significantly more suited to a sarcastic context than L2s did.
Taken with the above, L1s appear to see a greater overlap between sarcasm and positivity than L2 participants.
This could indicate that some of the meanings or uses of sarcasm are acquired earlier or are easier to access than others, hence L2 speakers tend to interpret sarcasm differently from L1 speakers.

If so, the use of sarcasm for criticism (Adams, 2012) may be an aspect that is acquired earlier, while other more positive aspects, such as humour or playfulness (Roberts & Kreuz, 1994) or softening the impact of a message (Dews & Winner, 1995; Harris & Pexman, 2003) come later.

text.text: This connects with the earlier discussion of the ;) emoticon: if playfulness is seen as an aspect of sarcasm by L1s but not by L2s, this would explain why the playful wink element is interpreted by L1s as a marker of sarcasm.
A broader pattern of divergence involves the upright-oriented kaomoji.

Across all context types, L2 participants were consistently more likely to use kaomoji than L1s, and also gave them consistently higher suitability ratings, though these patterns were not always statistically significant.

This broadly lines up with previous research on preferences for leftrotated emoticons versus kaomoji (Park et al., 2014), though the present findings cannot be attributed specifically to factors such as culture or language script.

text.text: Our findings reveal how certain types of visual variation within emoticons influence their meaning interpretation, while others do not.

This is not a factor that is easily measured by the scale of visual difference: some visually obvious changes, such as the addition of a nose element, have minimal effect on meaning; other visually minor changes, such as from colon to semicolon for the eyes, drastically impact perceived meaning.
The lowest impact comes from the nose element and from rotating an emoticon, while the greatest impact is produced by the eyes and mouth elements, as well as mirroring an emoticon.
The lower impact of rotation versus mirroring is comparable with established processing preferences in textual reading.

Understanding the ways different emoticon elements interact with meaning should be useful for translation software, sentiment analysis, natural language processing, and language teaching, especially in terms of digital literacy.
The current findings should, however, be expanded with further studies that include additional context types and a wider range of emoticon variations.
We also saw that native and non-native users of English pattern very closely in their overarching usage and meaning interpretation.
It has previously been established that emoticons are efficient markers of intention.
From the present study, we see this holds true in a second language, suggesting emoticons are a valid tool for facilitating conversations in cross-cultural and cross-linguistic contexts.
Importantly, there are exceptions to this, primarily for more subtle variations in emoticons and contexts.
While emoticons are considered non-linguistic and independent of any single language, they are still conventionalised within given language communities.
Their precise usage within a particular language context needs to be acquired alongside the rest of that language.
In a highly digital age, this is an important consideration for language learning and digital literacy.

While our study included a large sample of non-native speakers, further studies that focus on particular languages and cultures would be required to determine whether the observed effects are modulated by language-specific factors, such as the script of the L1 (logographic, abugida, abjad), or cultural factors, such as attitudes towards humour or emotional expression.
The present findings have several limitations to bear in mind.

Although participants were asked to judge broad context types rather than individual messages, the illustrative example that was provided for each context type may have influenced how that context was interpreted.

Since the investigation of variation was exploratory, the current study used frequently occurring emoticon variants identified in previous research, rather than systematically manipulating each possible visual feature.

Future studies could systematically manipulate nose, eyes, mouth, rotation, and mirroring, as well as other features, and could examine the possible additive effects of emoticons that contain multiple variations.

Although all emoticons included in the current study were identified as frequently occuring in production, this does not necessarily rule out influences from item-level familiarity or related traits; controlling for such factors in future work will require extensive norming, and ideally per-participant ratings.

Further research could explore the impact of participant variables, such as how L2 participants differ in terms of English proficiency, first language, writing system, and cultural background, and how L1 participants differ in aspects such as knowledge of other languages.
